newsitem.title: GERMANY: German economy strengthens with exports -Rexrodt.
newsitem.headline: German economy strengthens with exports -Rexrodt.

text.p: The German economy is gathering strength thanks to booming exports, and unemployment is set to begin falling convincingly from its recent postwar record levels, Economics Minister Guenter Rexrodt said on Monday.
The lower mark is bolstering exports, allowing Germany to boost its share of world markets, without fuelling the threat of imported inflation, he said.
Joblessness, while higher this year, should begin to shrink in 1998 as companies reach the point where they can only increase output by hiring new workers.

Rexrodt said gross domestic product grew as much as one percent in the second quarter from the previous quarter, and 2.5 to 3.0 percent from a year earlier. Second-quarter GDP data is due to be released on September 10.
Germany is on track to meet its forecast of nearly 2.5 percent growth this year, as GDP expanded by around two percent in the first half of 1997 compared to a year ago, he said.
"The positive economic trend has accelerated thanks to booming exports, and on the horizon the long-awaited turn in the labour market can be seen," Rexrodt said.
All in all, Germany's economy is on track to allow it to qualify for European economic and monetary union, he said.

"We will meet the criteria," he said. He attributed the mark's relative weakness against the dollar and the pound to a correction of its previous over-valuation, and the fact that Germany was in a different phase of its economic cycle than the U.S. and Britain.

He said the government expects growth to rise to 2.5 to 3.0 percent next year, and that German exports, which have been fuelling economic recovery, will grow faster than world trade, increasing Germany's share of world markets.
Rexrodt said he saw no inflationary dangers to the economy. Productivity has been rising while unit-labour costs have been falling, and recent wage agreements have been moderate.
Unemployment in 1997 will average 4.3 million, up 350,000 from last year, he said, adding that the government expected a decline of 100,000 in 1998.
Low interest rates, stable prices and high capacity utilisation should soon nudge manufacturers to increase investment, which will help the flagging domestic economy.
"The point is approaching at which more production can only be achieved with more personnel," he said.
In east Germany, weakness in the construction sector will continue to weigh on overall economic growth, but an upwsing in industrial activity is a bright sign, he said.
